dataset_family: NCGG-SGS (National Center for Geriatrics and Gerontology - Study of Geriatric Syndromes), Obu City, Aichi, Japan: community-dwelling adults aged 65+, first wave 2011-2012, second wave 2015-2016; 769 with MCI at the first wave (256 reverters / 395 maintainers / 118 converters after imputation)
method_family: Longitudinal community cohort: latent class analysis of 4-year lifestyle-activity change, then multinomial logistic regression of 4-year outcome (reverter / maintainer / converter) on class membership, with continuous GDS-15 entered only as an adjustment covariate; one-way ANOVA baseline comparison across outcome groups. At the evidence level for VF-27, its crude part is a baseline depression-scale comparison across MCI outcome groups (the same kind of analysis as P-647, P-788 and P-974); its adjusted part is a covariate coefficient in a model built for another exposure
what_it_shows: In 769 community-dwelling Japanese older adults with MCI, baseline GDS-15 differed across 4-year outcome groups in the crude comparison (reverters 2.6, maintainers 3.0, converters 3.3; one-way ANOVA p < 0.05; post hoc only reverters < converters). In the adjusted multinomial model (age, sex, education, smoking, heart and pulmonary disease, hypertension, diabetes, walking speed, MMSE and lifestyle-change class), GDS had OR 1.00 (0.91-1.10) for maintainers and 1.01 (0.90-1.13) for reverters, both p > 0.05. GDS is a covariate, not the exposure. 'Converter' means global cognitive impairment on an MMSE cut-off of < 24 and/or AD, not dementia conversion as such. 325 of 769 (42%) lacked the second-wave examination and were multiply imputed. No brain measure; every participant had MCI.
why: Katayama et al., Arch Gerontol Geriatr 94 (2021) 104376, DOI 10.1016/j.archger.2021.104376. The PDF title, authors and DOI match the summaries.md block and the map entry. Against the Table A1 statement the conversion limb is shown only in part. The adjusted model finds no independent association of continuous GDS-15 with 4-year outcome (ORs 1.00 and 1.01), which is consonant with 'continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'. But the paper's own crude comparison shows that GDS DID track outcome: converters scored higher than reverters (3.3 vs 2.6, p < 0.05, post hoc R<C). So the sentence is not true of this study without qualification, and the crude result is the reverse of P-647's crude null (5.54 vs 5.73, p = 0.859). The adjusted null also conditions on MMSE and on the lifestyle class, and GDS itself differs by class (Table 3: class 3 4.0 vs classes 1 and 2 at 2.7 and 2.3, p < 0.001), so the model may absorb part of the depression signal. GDS was never the exposure, and no GDS-specific analysis is reported. The multinomial reference outcome is not named in Table 5; by elimination it is converters. Further limits: the 'converter' outcome is GCI on an MMSE cut-off of < 24 and/or AD, not all-cause dementia; 42% attrition was handled by multivariate normal imputation, and Table 1 is the imputed sample; Table 5 prints walking speed 6.89 (1.87-25.30) with 'p > 0.05', an internal inconsistency that does not touch the GDS rows, whose CIs straddle 1. Not tested: the first clause (all participants have MCI), the brain-measure limb and the 'although' clause. Round-1 standard: P-1326 was 'partly' because its continuous GDS tracked conversion in the crude comparison while its adjusted and stratified analyses were null; P-671 shows the same pattern, with the crude association in the expected direction. It cannot be a 'yes'. Independence: NCGG-SGS (Obu, Japan) is not the dataset of any current supporter (P-643 Korea University Guro; P-647 Shanghai Brain Health Cohort; P-662 Shanghai Tongji; P-663 Florence) or of any round-1 or round-2 candidate, and no authors are shared. Not a preprint. Quotes are transliterated to ASCII (- for en dashes, straight apostrophes).

quotes.quote: Of the 769 participants, 325 did not undergo the second-wave cognitive examination (Fig. 1). Because potential bias was identified in the first-wave data as a result of the sample size of those remaining, from lost to follow-up, we used multivariate normal imputation to adjust for the selection bias and information loss
the converters were those who had GCI; as indicated by the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) (Folstein, Folstein & McHugh, 1975) cutoff score of <24 points (O'Bryant et al., 2008).
Participants were allocated to the following three groups: reverters who had NC at the follow-up; maintainers who maintained MCI; and converters who had GCI and/or AD at the follow-up.

Unadjusted and adjusted models included the following covariates: participants' age, sex, educational qualification, current smoking, heart disease, pulmonary disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, walking speed, MMSE score, and 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) (Yesavage, 1988) score(Katayama et al., 2020).
There were significant differences between the groups in age, gender, educational qualifications, walking speed, MMSE score, GDS score, MCI status, and life activities (Table 1).

our study did not use random sampling for data collection, and about 42% of participants were lost to follow-up; hence, under-reporting is possible of the incidence rate of MCI and GCI among older adults.
